R_H1.passageTitle: A New Way to Carry Astronauts

passages.label: A
passages.text: On 30 May 2020, two NASA astronauts left Florida in SpaceX's Crew Dragon. The project linked a public agency with a private company. Its goal was to provide transport to the International Space Station. The flight advanced a programme in which NASA and a company had different jobs. For an entrepreneur, building a ship is one part of the task. The ship must also meet the conditions NASA sets for carrying its staff.

passages.label: B
passages.text: NASA had once owned the machines and told its partners much more about how to build them. Under the Commercial Crew plan, firms owned the machines and ran their own flights. NASA could still give advice and evaluate the work. It also set rules for keeping people safe. The plan was meant to make return trips possible so people could go on doing research on the station.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Tests came before regular passenger missions. NASA wanted to evaluate a spacecraft before relying on it for a human journey. An expert might check an issue such as what happens if a launch stops, because every new option needs a solution to an unexpected problem. Test flights help engineers separate one effect from another. The experience of sending a satellite into orbit gives useful knowledge, while a vehicle with people on board has to meet extra requirements.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Demo-2 brought astronauts into the test programme. They launched in May and returned to Earth on 2 August 2020. Engineers then examined the flight data to inform the approval review. In November, NASA approved the SpaceX system for regular journeys with crews. That approval covered the spacecraft, rocket and associated equipment on the ground. It followed years of development and testing. Teams had also tested parachutes and practised rescuing crews in an emergency. These preparations connected the work of designers with the needs of people who would actually use the system. The review considered a particular transport system, rather than giving automatic permission to every spacecraft that a company might build. Some people believe one successful flight is enough to settle the question. Engineers still assess the evidence, because they have to decide which checks remain.

passages.label: E
passages.text: These journeys support research at the station. Reports from test flights give NASA evidence about a particular ship under particular conditions. And the agency can study those results before making a decision. Missions beyond the station call for other work. Making advances in one type of flight does not prove that a ship is ready to explore a more distant place.

R_H2.passageTitle: When a Space Delivery Comes Back

passages.label: A
passages.text: On 15 April 2023, a spacecraft splashed down off Florida with experiments and other cargo from the International Space Station. Researchers planned to examine samples before Earth's gravity fully affected them. There were no people inside this cargo Dragon. Its return gave scientists on Earth materials they could study after work in orbit. A space delivery was therefore a journey in two directions. Taking supplies up was important, but bringing results down also served a particular purpose.

passages.label: B
passages.text: One returning experiment concerned tomatoes grown in the station's small greenhouse. Astronauts had collected three harvests and frozen tomatoes, water samples and samples taken from the growing equipment. Researchers wanted to examine how light and fertiliser affected the crops. The conditions of growing plants in space mattered for future long journeys. This work went beyond the simple question of whether a seed could grow. It also concerned the quality and safety of food for people. Two samples can look much the same when they return to Earth. A note about where each one grew tells the team which one spent time in space.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Other materials addressed different problems. Blood samples returned from an investigation of changes in astronauts' blood vessels. Samples from a fire experiment were also on board. That experiment examined how flames grow and go out in very weak gravity. NASA's report described possible uses for this work, including safer materials inside spacecraft. The aim was to support better decisions about safety, rather than to assume that every material behaved in space exactly as it did on Earth. NASA also described possible benefits for people on Earth. Investigating changes in blood vessels, for example, could help researchers understand health problems connected with growing older, as well as space travel.

passages.label: D
passages.text: A returning spacecraft gives researchers an option that a vehicle without a return journey cannot offer. An alternative may be to send results by radio, yet a physical sample lets an expert examine an effect in more detail. Researchers can evaluate a possible problem and look for a solution with equipment that did not fly. The impact of a delay can vary with the type of sample.

passages.label: E
passages.text: NASA bought these services from private companies to support public research. A report can help people study a particular sample. People may wonder whether the data sent from space can prove the same thing as a sample. There may be differences that only exist under certain conditions. Bringing samples home is an advance that helps scientists check those differences. The two methods can suggest new questions and give different kinds of evidence.

R_H3.passageTitle: What a Spotted Mars Rock Can Tell Us

passages.label: A
passages.text: In July 2024, NASA's Perseverance rover examined a rock in an ancient river valley on Mars. Scientists called the rock Cheyava Falls. Its pale patches, surrounded by darker material, looked rather like leopard spots, and the rover collected a sample and used instruments to study the rock. These observations became evidence for an investigation of a large question: did tiny living things once exist on Mars? The shape of the spots alone did not provide a complete answer.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The rock contained carbon-based materials and minerals that interested the team. On Earth, some similar chemical changes can be connected with tiny organisms obtaining energy. This comparison could suggest a possible connection with life on Mars, but the same minerals can also form without living things. Scientists needed to consider several explanations, rather than choose a biological one because it sounded exciting, and the question concerned the processes that made the rock, not simply whether it looked unusual.

passages.label: C
passages.text: In September 2025, NASA described the sample as containing potential biosignatures, and a biosignature is a sign connected with life, and the word potential means that more information is needed. Scientists could believe that an explanation deserved attention without claiming it was already certain. Their research had reached a stage where observations could be examined and questioned by other specialists, and the announcement did not say that the rover had seen an organism moving across the surface of Mars. A possible sign can concern life in the distant past, and it need not demonstrate that something is alive in the same place at the time of observation.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The team also looked at explanations involving heat and acidic conditions, and the rocks did not show signs of the high temperatures or acidity involved in some non-biological explanations. This made those explanations less likely in the reported work, but it did not prove that life was the cause. Scientists said they could not rule out processes without life. A possibility that seems unlikely still needs consideration when the conclusion would change our understanding of another planet. An expert can evaluate an alternative explanation for this planet. Comparing surface patterns is one option. A sample might clarify a chemical issue and show which problem needs a different test.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The rover could study the sample with equipment on Mars. A public report on the 2024 examination explains why a laboratory on Earth could take the work beyond that first set of tests. A more detailed test would be a particular advance for scientists who want to explore whether the spots support one explanation more than another. People still wonder about life elsewhere, but a new question and evidence that can prove a claim are different stages of research.
